concept.name: Multi-Agent Orchestration

relationships.description: Connects Multi-Agent Orchestration to llm prompt engineering in the broader engineering catalog.

concept.tagline: Coordinating specialized LLM agents with scoped tools and filtered JSON handoffs via supervisor graphs, swarms, or DAGs.
concept.purpose: Prevent tool-selection degradation and context bloat by isolating agent responsibilities, enforcing hard iteration budgets, and passing structured artifacts.

spark.summary: Multi-agent orchestration coordinates specialized LLM agents—each with scoped prompts, tools, and memory—using explicit control topologies like supervisor graphs, handoff swarms, or DAG pipelines.
spark.keyTakeaway: Isolate responsibilities across specialized sub-agents with narrow toolsets, pass compact structured JSON artifacts instead of raw 20 KB tool dumps, and enforce hard step/token budgets on every cycle.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** **Multi-agent orchestration** splits complex AI workflows across specialized agents—each with its own scoped system prompt, narrow toolset (3–7 tools), and isolated working memory—coordinated via a **supervisor graph**.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Supervisor Delegating to Scoped Specialist Agents (Supervisor -> Read-Only SQL -> Research Agent -> Action Agent); Supervisor State Machine with Loop Detection & Escalation (SUPERVISOR -> SPECIALIST -> ESCALATE).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Topology and state-passing choices govern predictability and token spend. A single LLM prompt degrades sharply once tool schemas exceed ~15–20 definitions or mixed history crosses 30k–50k tokens.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore HITL supervisor workflows, LangGraph state machines, and MCP tool servers.

learningJourney.title: What is Multi-Agent Orchestration
learningJourney.explanation:
**Multi-agent orchestration** splits complex AI workflows across specialized agents—each with its own scoped system prompt, narrow toolset (3–7 tools), and isolated working memory—coordinated via a **supervisor graph**, **peer-to-peer handoff swarm**, or **parallel fan-out DAG**.

Instead of forwarding 20 KB of raw prose and tool payloads between agents, orchestrators pass **compact structured JSON artifacts** and canonical IDs.

sectionDiagram.summary: Scoping each specialist to 3–7 tools keeps tool-selection accuracy high and enforces least-privilege permissions.

learningJourney.title: Why 40-tool monolith prompts fail—and how ping-pong loops happen
learningJourney.explanation:
A single LLM prompt degrades sharply once tool schemas exceed ~15–20 definitions or mixed history crosses 30k–50k tokens.

However, multi-agent systems introduce two new failure modes: **Infinite Critique / Ping-Pong Loops** (Writer and Reviewer bounce control until the API bill spikes) and **Telephone-Game Context Loss** (each agent re-summarizes constraints in prose, silently dropping a critical filter like `exclude EU accounts`).

ideas.title: Immutable Top-Level Constraints
ideas.description: Keep canonical IDs and user filters in a typed top-level state object that every agent reads directly rather than relying on prose summaries.

ideas.title: Hard Step & Cycle Detection
ideas.description: Enforce `max_iterations` (e.g., 8–12), token budgets, and state-hash cycle detection to escalate to a human or fallback.

comparison.choice: Good Candidate: Cross-Domain Security & Parallel Fan-Out
benefits: Separates read-only SQL analytics from write-scoped Jira/GitHub mutations, or fans out across 10 research targets.

comparison.choice: Avoid: Single-Call Tasks or Deterministic ETL
benefits: Use one model call with 2–5 tools (<3 s) or Temporal/Airflow for deterministic pipelines.
costs: Multi-agent routing adds unnecessary cost and variance.

learningJourney.title: Filtered JSON Handoffs & Step-Budget Guardrails
learningJourney.explanation: Store immutable constraints at the root of `OrchestratorState`, cap `steps_remaining`, and pass structured Pydantic artifacts between agents.
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Supervisor Graph vs. Decentralized Swarm vs. Filtered vs. Shared Scratchpad
learningJourney.explanation: Topology and state-passing choices govern predictability and token spend.

benefits: Deterministic routing, clear audit trails, and centralized cost/step ceilings.
costs: Supervisor LLM call adds one routing hop per turn.

benefits: Lower hop count between adjacent specialists.
costs: Harder to debug cycles and enforce global policy without a central router.

comparison.choice: Filtered JSON Handoffs vs. Shared Scratchpad
benefits: Cuts token costs by 50–80% and isolates downstream agents from prompt injection.
costs: Over-aggressive summarization can drop subtle edge-case details.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Checkpointed Supervisor + Least-Privilege Subgraphs
learningJourney.explanation: Production multi-agent platforms run each specialist inside a least-privilege **MCP / tool sandbox**, persist root state in Postgres after every hop, and emit OpenTelemetry spans per agent transition to track token burn and loop counts.

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
